paragraphs: “Let the red dawn guess What we shall do, When this blue starlight dies And all is over.”
I

There are so many things that cannot be explained! Why should certain musical chords make me think of the brown and gold of autumn leaves? Why should the Mass of Sainte Cécile send my thoughts wandering through caverns whose walls blaze with jagged masses of pure silver? What was it in the roar and turmoil of Broadway at six o’clock that flashed a picture before my eyes of a still Breton forest? Sunlight filtered through the spring leaves, and Sylvia bent, half curious, half tender, over a little green lizard, murmuring, “To think that this too is a little creature in God’s care!”

When I first saw the watchman, his back was towards me. I looked at him without interest until he went into the church. I paid him no more attention than any other man strolling through Washington Square that morning. When I closed my window and turned back into my studio, I had forgotten him. Late that afternoon, because the day was warm, I opened the window again and leaned out for a breath of air. A man stood in the church courtyard, and I noticed him again with as little interest as that morning. I looked across the square towards the playing fountain. Then, my mind full of vague impressions of trees, asphalt drives and moving groups of nursemaids and holidaymakers, I began to walk back to my easel. As I turned, my idle glance took in the man below in the churchyard. His face was towards me now, and quite involuntarily I bent to see it. At the same moment, he raised his head and looked at me. Instantly I thought of a coffin-worm. I did not know what it was about him that repelled me, but the impression of a plump, white grave-worm was so intense and sickening that it must have shown on my face. He turned his puffy face away with a movement that reminded me of a grub disturbed inside a chestnut.

I returned to my easel and motioned to the model to resume her pose. After working for a while, I became certain that I was ruining my work as quickly as possible. I picked up a palette knife and scraped the colour off again. The flesh tones were yellowish and unhealthy. I could not understand how I had painted such sickly colour into a study that, until then, had glowed with healthy tones.
I looked at Tessie. She had not changed. As I frowned, the clear flush of health coloured her neck and cheeks.
“Is it something I’ve done?” she asked.
“No—I’ve made a mess of this arm, and for the life of me I can’t see how I came to paint such mud onto the canvas,” I replied.
“Am I not posing well?” she insisted.
“Of course you are. Perfectly.”
“Then it isn’t my fault?”
“No. It’s mine.”
“I’m very sorry,” she said.
I told her she could rest while I worked on the diseased spot on my canvas with a rag and turpentine. She went off to smoke a cigarette and look through the illustrations in the Courrier Français.

I did not know whether something was wrong with the turpentine or the canvas, but the more I scrubbed, the more that gangrene seemed to spread. I worked like a beaver to remove it, yet the disease appeared to creep from limb to limb of the study before me. Alarmed, I struggled to stop it. But now the colour on the chest changed, and the whole figure seemed to absorb the infection as a sponge soaks up water. I worked vigorously with palette knife, turpentine and scraper, thinking all the time what a scene I would have with Duval, who had sold me the canvas. Soon, however, I noticed that neither the canvas nor Edward’s paints were defective. “It must be the turpentine,” I thought angrily, “or else the afternoon light has blurred and confused my eyes so much that I can’t see straight.” I called Tessie, the model. She came and leaned over my chair, blowing smoke rings into the air.
“What have you been doing to it?” she exclaimed.
“Nothing,” I growled. “It must be this turpentine!”
“What a horrible colour it is now,” she continued. “Do you think my flesh looks like green cheese?”
“No, I don’t,” I said angrily. “Have you ever known me to paint like that before?”
“Certainly not!”
“Well, then!”
“It must be the turpentine, or something,” she admitted.

She put on a Japanese robe and walked to the window. I scraped and rubbed until I was tired. Finally I picked up my brushes and hurled them through the canvas with a forceful expression. Only its tone reached Tessie’s ears.

Nevertheless, she promptly began, “That’s it! Swear and act silly and ruin your brushes! You’ve spent three weeks on that study, and now look! What good does it do to rip the canvas? What creatures artists are!”

I felt about as ashamed as I usually did after such an outburst and turned the ruined canvas towards the wall. Tessie helped me clean my brushes, then danced away to dress. From behind the screen she treated me to pieces of advice about losing all or part of one’s temper. At last, perhaps thinking she had tormented me enough, she came out and begged me to fasten her blouse where she could not reach the buttons on her shoulder.
“Everything went wrong from the moment you came back from the window and talked about that horrible-looking man in the churchyard,” she announced.
“Yes, he probably bewitched the picture,” I said, yawning. I looked at my watch.
“I know it’s after six,” Tessie said, adjusting her hat in front of the mirror.

“Yes,” I replied. “I didn’t mean to keep you so long.” I leaned out of the window but recoiled in disgust. The young man with the pasty face was standing below in the churchyard. Tessie saw my gesture of disapproval and leaned out of the window.
“Is that the man you don’t like?” she whispered.
I nodded.

“I can’t see his face, but he does look fat and soft. Somehow or other,” she continued, turning to me, “he reminds me of a dream—an awful dream I once had. Or,” she wondered, looking down at her shapely shoes, “was it a dream after all?”
“How should I know?” I said, smiling.
Tessie smiled in return.
“You were in it,” she said, “so perhaps you might know something about it.”
“Tessie! Tessie!” I protested. “Don’t you dare flatter me by saying you dream about me!”
“But I did,” she insisted. “Shall I tell you about it?”
“Go ahead,” I replied, lighting a cigarette.
Tessie leaned back against the open windowsill and began very seriously.

“One night last winter, I was lying in bed thinking of nothing in particular. I had been posing for you and was worn out, yet I seemed unable to sleep. I heard the city bells strike ten, eleven and midnight. I must have fallen asleep around midnight, because I don’t remember hearing them after that. It seemed I had barely closed my eyes when I dreamed that something drove me to the window. I got up, raised the sash and leaned out. Twenty-fifth Street was deserted as far as I could see. I began to feel afraid. Everything outside seemed so—so black and unsettling. Then I heard wheels in the distance, and it seemed that this was what I had to wait for. Very slowly the wheels approached. At last I could make out a vehicle moving along the street. It came nearer and nearer. When it passed beneath my window, I saw that it was a hearse. As I trembled with fear, the driver turned and looked straight at me. When I woke, I was standing beside the open window, shivering with cold. But the hearse with its black plumes and its driver had gone. I had the same dream again last March and again woke beside the open window. Last night the dream came again. You remember how it was raining. When I woke, standing at the open window, my nightdress was soaked.”
“But where did I come into the dream?” I asked.
“You—you were in the coffin. But you weren’t dead.”
“In the coffin?”
“Yes.”
“How did you know? Could you see me?”
“No. I just knew you were there.”
“Had you been eating Welsh rarebit, or lobster salad?” I began, laughing. But she interrupted me with a frightened cry.
“Hello! What’s the matter?” I asked as she shrank into the window recess.
“The—the man down in the churchyard—he drove the hearse.”

“Nonsense,” I said, but Tessie’s eyes were wide with terror. I went to the window and looked out. The man had gone. “Come on, Tessie,” I urged. “Don’t be foolish. You’ve been posing too long. You’re nervous.”

“Do you think I could forget that face?” she murmured. “Three times I saw the hearse pass below my window, and every time the driver turned and looked up at me. Oh, his face was so white and—and soft? It looked dead. It looked as though it had been dead a long time.”
I persuaded her to sit down and drink a glass of Marsala. Then I sat beside her and tried to give her some advice.

“Listen, Tessie,” I said. “Go to the country for a week or two, and you’ll stop dreaming about hearses. You pose all day, and by night your nerves are upset. You can’t keep this up. Besides, instead of going to bed when your day’s work is done, you run off to picnics at Sulzer’s Park, or to the Eldorado or Coney Island. Then you come here the next morning exhausted. There was no real hearse. It was a dream brought on by soft-shell crab.”
She smiled faintly.
“What about the man in the churchyard?”
“Oh, he’s just an ordinary, unhealthy, everyday creature.”
“As surely as my name is Tessie Reardon, I swear to you, Mr Scott, that the man down in the churchyard has the face of the man who drove the hearse!”
“What of it?” I said. “It’s an honest trade.”
“Then you think I did see the hearse?”
“Oh,” I said diplomatically, “if you really did, it’s quite possible the man below drove it. There’s nothing in that.”

Tessie stood up and unrolled her scented handkerchief. She took a piece of chewing gum from a knot in its hem and put it in her mouth. Then she drew on her gloves, offered me her hand with a frank “Goodnight, Mr Scott,” and walked out.
II

The next morning, Thomas, the bellboy, brought me the Herald and a piece of news. The church next door had been sold. I thanked Heaven. I was Catholic, but had no dislike of the neighbouring congregation. But my nerves had been shattered by a loud preacher whose every word echoed through the church aisle as though it were in my own rooms. He dwelt on his r’s with a nasal persistence that offended every instinct I had. Then there was a fiend in human form, an organist who rattled through some of the grand old hymns with his own interpretation. I thirsted for the blood of a creature who could play the doxology with added minor chords of the sort heard only in a quartet of very young undergraduates. I believe the minister was a good man. But when he bellowed, “And the Lorrrrd said to Moses, the Lorrrd is a man of war; the Lorrrd is his name. My anger shall burn hot, and I will kill you with the sworrrrd!” I wondered how many centuries in purgatory would atone for such a sin.
“Who bought the property?” I asked Thomas.
“Nobody I know, sir. They say the gentleman who owns these Hamilton flats was looking at it. He might be building more studios.”
I walked to the window. The young man with the unhealthy face stood by the churchyard gate. The mere sight of him filled me with the same overwhelming disgust.
“By the way, Thomas,” I said, “who is that fellow down there?”

Thomas sniffed. “That worm, sir? He’s the church’s night watchman, sir. I’m sick of him sitting on those steps all night, looking at you as though he’s insulting you. I’d have punched his head, sir—beg your pardon, sir—”
“Go on, Thomas.”

“One night, coming home with Harry, the other English boy, I saw him sitting there on those steps. We had Molly and Jen with us, sir, the two girls who serve the trays. He looked at us so insultingly that I spoke up: ‘What are you looking at, you fat slug?’ Beg your pardon, sir, but that’s what I said, sir. He didn’t say anything, so I said, ‘Come out and I’ll punch that pudding head.’ Then I opened the gate and went in. Still he said nothing, just looked at me insultingly. So I hit him once. But ugh! His head was so cold and mushy it would make you sick to touch him.”
“What did he do then?” I asked curiously.
“Him? Nothing.”
“And you, Thomas?”
The young man flushed with embarrassment and smiled uneasily.
“Mr Scott, sir, I’m no coward, and I can’t understand at all why I ran. I was in the 5th Lancers, sir, a bugler at Tel-el-Kebir, and I was shot by the wells.”
“You don’t mean you ran away?”
“Yes, sir. I ran.”
“Why?”
“That’s just what I want to know, sir. I grabbed Molly and ran, and the rest were as frightened as I was.”
“But what were they frightened of?”

For a while Thomas refused to answer. But now the repulsive young man below had aroused my curiosity, and I pressed him. Three years in America had not only changed Thomas’s Cockney dialect; they had also given him the American fear of ridicule.
“You won’t believe me, Mr Scott, sir?”
“Yes, I will.”
“You’ll laugh at me, sir?”
“Nonsense!”
He hesitated. “Well, sir, it’s God’s truth. When I hit him, he grabbed my wrists, sir. And when I twisted his soft, mushy fist, one of his fingers came off in my hand.”
The utter loathing and horror on Thomas’s face must have been reflected in mine, for he added:
“It’s awful. Now, whenever I see him, I just go away. He makes me ill.”

After Thomas left, I went to the window. The man stood beside the church railings with both hands on the gate. But I hurried back to my easel, sickened and horrified: the middle finger of his right hand was missing.

At nine o’clock Tessie appeared and vanished behind the screen with a cheerful “Good morning, Mr Scott.” When she came out again and took her pose on the model’s platform, I began a new canvas, much to her delight. She stayed silent while I drew. But as soon as the scraping of the charcoal stopped and I picked up my fixative, she began to chatter.
“Oh, I had such a lovely time last night. We went to Tony Pastor’s.”
“Who are ‘we’?” I demanded.
“Oh, Maggie—you know, Mr Whyte’s model—and Pinkie McCormick. We call her Pinkie because she has that beautiful red hair you artists like so much. And Lizzie Burke.”
I sprayed a shower of fixative over the canvas and said, “Well, go on.”
“We saw Kelly and Baby Barnes, the skirt dancer, and—and all the rest. I found an admirer.”
“So you’ve deserted me, Tessie?”
She laughed and shook her head.
“He’s Lizzie Burke’s brother, Ed. He’s a perfect gentleman.”
I felt obliged to give her some fatherly advice about flirtations, which she accepted with a bright smile.
“Oh, I can manage an admirer I don’t know,” she said, examining her chewing gum. “But Ed is different. Lizzie is my best friend.”

Then she told me how Ed had returned from the stocking mill in Lowell, Massachusetts, to find her and Lizzie grown up. She described what an accomplished young man he was, and how he thought nothing of squandering half a dollar on ice cream and oysters to celebrate becoming a clerk in Macy’s woollen department. Before she finished, I began to paint, and she resumed her pose, smiling and chattering like a sparrow. By noon I had laid in the study fairly well, and Tessie came to look at it.
“That’s better,” she said.

I thought so too and ate my lunch with the satisfied feeling that everything was going well. Tessie spread her lunch on a drawing table opposite me. We drank claret from the same bottle and lit our cigarettes from the same match. I was very fond of Tessie. I had watched her grow rapidly from a frail, awkward child into a slender woman with an exquisitely formed body. She had posed for me for the past three years, and she was my favourite of all my models. It would have troubled me very much if she had become “rough” or “worldly,” as people say. But I had never noticed her manners getting worse and felt in my heart that she was all right. We never discussed morals, and I had no intention of doing so. Partly this was because I had none myself, and partly because I knew she would do as she pleased despite me. Still, I hoped she would avoid complications, because I wished her well. I also had a selfish desire to keep my best model. I knew that what she called flirtation had no significance for girls like Tessie, and that these things in America were quite unlike the same things in Paris. Yet I had lived with my eyes open. I also knew that, one way or another, someone would take Tessie away one day. Though I told myself that marriage was nonsense, I sincerely hoped that, in this case, there would be a priest at the end of that vista. I am a Catholic. When I listen to high mass, when I make the sign of the cross, I feel that everything, including myself, is more cheerful. Confession does me good. A man who lives as much alone as I do must confess to someone. Besides, Sylvia was Catholic, which was reason enough for me. But I was speaking of Tessie, which is very different. Tessie was Catholic too, and much more devout than I was. Taking everything together, I had little fear for my pretty model until she fell in love. Then I knew that fate alone would decide her future. I prayed inwardly that fate would keep her away from men like me and put only Ed Burkes and Jimmy McCormicks in her path, bless her sweet face!
Tessie sat blowing smoke rings towards the ceiling and tinkling the ice in her tumbler.
“Do you know I had a dream last night too?” I remarked.
“Not about that man,” she said, laughing.
“Exactly. A dream like yours, only much worse.”

It was foolish and thoughtless of me to say this, but you know how little tact the average painter has. “I must have fallen asleep around ten,” I continued. “After a while, I dreamed that I woke up. I heard the midnight bells, the wind in the tree branches, and the whistles of steamers in the bay so clearly that even now I can hardly believe I wasn’t awake. I seemed to be lying in a box with a glass lid. Dimly I saw street lamps passing. I must explain, Tessie, that the box I lay in seemed to rest in a cushioned wagon that jolted me over a stony road. After a while I grew impatient and tried to move, but the box was too narrow. My hands were crossed on my chest, so I couldn’t raise them to help myself. I listened, then tried to call out. My voice was gone. I could hear the trampling of the horses pulling the wagon, and even the driver’s breathing. Then I heard another sound, like a window sash being raised. I managed to turn my head a little. I found I could look not only through the glass lid of my box but also through the glass panes in the side of the covered vehicle. I saw empty, silent houses. None showed any light or life, except one. In that house a first-floor window was open, and a figure dressed entirely in white stood looking down into the street. It was you.”
Tessie had turned her face away and leaned her elbow on the table.

“I could see your face,” I continued, “and it seemed very sorrowful. Then we went on and turned into a narrow, black lane. Before long, the horses stopped. I waited and waited, closing my eyes in fear and impatience, but everything was as silent as the grave. After what seemed like hours, I began to feel uneasy. I sensed someone close to me and opened my eyes. Then I saw the hearse driver’s white face looking at me through the coffin lid—”
A sob from Tessie interrupted me. She was trembling like a leaf. I realised I had made an ass of myself and tried to undo the damage.

“Why, Tess,” I said, “I only told you to show how your story could influence someone else’s dreams. You don’t suppose I really lay in a coffin, do you? Why are you trembling? Don’t you see? Your dream and my unreasonable dislike of that harmless church watchman simply set my brain working as soon as I fell asleep.”

She buried her head in her arms and sobbed as though her heart would break. What a perfect triple donkey I had made of myself! But I was about to surpass my own record. I went over and put my arm around her.
“Dear Tessie, forgive me,” I said. “I had no right to frighten you with such nonsense. You’re too sensible a girl, too good a Catholic, to believe in dreams.”
Her hand tightened on mine and her head fell back against my shoulder. Still she trembled, and I caressed and comforted her.
“Come on, Tess. Open your eyes and smile.”
Her eyes opened slowly and languidly and met mine. But their expression was so strange that I hurried to reassure her again.
“It’s all nonsense, Tessie. Surely you aren’t afraid any harm will come to you because of it.”
“No,” she said, but her scarlet lips trembled.
“Then what’s wrong? Are you afraid?”
“Yes. Not for myself.”
“For me, then?” I asked cheerfully.
“For you,” she murmured, almost too softly to hear. “I—I care for you.”

At first I began to laugh. But when I understood her, a shock went through me, and I sat as though turned to stone. This was the crowning act of stupidity I had committed. In the moment between her reply and my answer, I thought of a thousand responses to that innocent confession. I could laugh it away. I could misunderstand her and reassure her about my health. I could simply point out that she could not possibly love me. But my response was faster than my thoughts. Now I could think and think, when it was too late: I had kissed her on the mouth.

That evening I took my usual walk in Washington Park, thinking over the day’s events. I had committed myself completely. There was no backing out now, and I faced the future squarely. I was not a good man, not even a principled one, but I had no intention of deceiving either myself or Tessie. The one passion of my life lay buried in the sunlit forests of Brittany. Was it buried for ever? Hope cried, “No!” For three years I had listened to Hope’s voice, and for three years I had waited for a footstep on my threshold. Had Sylvia forgotten? “No!” cried Hope.

I said I was no good. That is true, but I was not exactly a villain from a comic opera. I had lived an easygoing, reckless life, taking whatever pleasure tempted me, deploring the consequences and sometimes regretting them bitterly. Apart from painting, I was serious about only one thing, and that lay hidden, if not lost, in the Breton forests.

It was too late to regret what had happened that day. Whatever had prompted it—pity, a sudden tenderness towards sorrow, or the more brutal instinct of satisfied vanity—it made no difference now. Unless I meant to bruise an innocent heart, my path was marked out before me. With all my imagined experience of the world, I had never even suspected the fire, strength and passionate depth of her love. It left me no choice but to respond or send her away. Perhaps I am cowardly about hurting others; perhaps I have little of the gloomy Puritan in me. I do not know. But I shrank from denying responsibility for that thoughtless kiss. In fact, before I had time to do so, the gates of her heart opened and the flood poured out. Others, who always do their duty and find sullen satisfaction in making themselves and everyone else unhappy, might have resisted it. I did not. I dared not. After the storm subsided, I did tell her she would have done better to love Ed Burke and wear a plain gold ring. But she would not hear of it. I thought that, since she had decided to love someone she could not marry, it might as well be me. At least I could treat her with intelligent affection. Whenever she tired of her infatuation, she could leave none the worse for it. I was determined on that point, though I knew how difficult it would be. I remembered how Platonic affairs usually ended, and how disgusted I had been whenever I heard of one. I knew I was taking on a great deal for a man as unscrupulous as I was. I dreamed of the future, but never for a moment doubted that she was safe with me. If it had been anyone but Tessie, I would not have troubled myself with scruples. It never occurred to me to sacrifice Tessie as I would have sacrificed a woman of the world. I faced the future squarely and saw the affair’s several likely endings. Either she would tire of the whole thing, or she would become so unhappy that I would have to marry her or go away. If I married her, we would both be unhappy: I with a wife unsuited to me, she with a husband unsuited to any woman. My past life could hardly entitle me to marry. If I went away, she might fall ill, recover and marry some Eddie Burke. Or, recklessly or deliberately, she might go and do something foolish. On the other hand, if she tired of me, her whole life would lie before her, with beautiful prospects of Eddie Burkes, wedding rings, twins, Harlem flats and Heaven knows what. As I strolled through the trees by the Washington Arch, I decided that, whatever happened, she would find a dependable friend in me. The future could take care of itself. Then I went into the house and put on my evening clothes. A little, faintly scented note on my dressing table said, “Have a cab at the stage door at eleven.” It was signed, “Edith Carmichel, Metropolitan Theatre.”

I had supper that night—or rather, Miss Carmichel and I had supper—at Solari’s. Dawn was just beginning to gild the cross on the Memorial Church when I entered Washington Square after leaving Edith at the Brunswick. There was not a soul in the park as I walked along the trees and took the path from the Garibaldi statue to the Hamilton Apartment House. But as I passed the churchyard, I saw a figure sitting on the stone steps. Despite myself, a chill crept over me at the sight of that white, puffy face, and I hurried past. Then he said something. It might have been addressed to me, or he might only have been muttering to himself. But a sudden, furious anger blazed inside me at the thought of such a creature speaking to me. For a moment I wanted to turn and smash my stick over his head. Instead, I walked on, entered the Hamilton and went to my apartment. For some time I tossed in bed, trying and failing to get the sound of his voice out of my ears. That muttering filled my head like thick, oily smoke from a vat of melting fat, or a stench of foul decay. As I lay tossing, the voice in my ears seemed to grow clearer, and I began to understand the words he had muttered. They came to me slowly, as though I had forgotten them. At last I could make sense of the sounds. This was what he had said:
“Have you found the Yellow Sign?”
“Have you found the Yellow Sign?”
“Have you found the Yellow Sign?”

I was furious. What did he mean? Then, with a curse on him and his, I rolled over and went to sleep. But when I woke later I looked pale and haggard. I had dreamed the previous night’s dream again, and it troubled me more than I cared to think.

I dressed and went down to my studio. Tessie was sitting by the window, but when I came in she stood up and put both arms around my neck for an innocent kiss. She looked so sweet and delicate that I kissed her again, then sat down in front of the easel.
“Hello! Where’s the study I began yesterday?” I asked.
Tessie looked self-conscious but did not answer. I began searching through the piles of canvases. “Hurry up, Tess, and get ready,” I said. “We must make use of the morning light.”
At last I gave up searching among the other canvases and turned to look around the room for the missing study. Then I noticed Tessie standing by the screen, still dressed.
“What’s wrong?” I asked. “Don’t you feel well?”
“Yes.”
“Then hurry.”
“Do you want me to pose as—as I always have?”

Then I understood. Here was a new complication. Of course, I had lost the best nude model I had ever seen. I looked at Tessie. Her face was scarlet. Alas! Alas! We had eaten from the tree of knowledge. Eden and natural innocence were dreams of the past—for her, I mean.
I suppose she noticed my disappointment, because she said, “I’ll pose if you want. The study is here behind the screen, where I put it.”

“No,” I said. “We’ll begin something new.” I went to my wardrobe and chose a Moorish costume that blazed with tinsel. It was an authentic costume, and Tessie took it behind the screen, delighted. When she came out again, I was astonished. Her long black hair was held above her forehead by a circlet of turquoise stones, its ends curling around her glittering belt. Her feet were covered by embroidered, pointed slippers. The skirt, intricately worked with silver arabesques, fell to her ankles. The deep metallic-blue vest embroidered with silver and the short Moorish jacket, spangled and sewn with turquoise stones, suited her wonderfully. She came up to me and raised her smiling face. I reached into my pocket, drew out a gold chain with a cross attached, and slipped it over her head.
“It’s yours, Tessie.”
“Mine?” she faltered.
“Yours. Now go and pose.” With a radiant smile, she ran behind the screen. Soon she reappeared with a little box bearing my name.
“I meant to give it to you when I went home tonight,” she said, “but now I can’t wait.”

I opened the box. On the pink cotton inside lay a black onyx clasp, inlaid with a strange gold symbol or letter. It was neither Arabic nor Chinese. As I later discovered, it belonged to no human writing system.
“It’s all I had to give you as a keepsake,” she said shyly.
I was annoyed, but I told her how much I would treasure it and promised to wear it always. She fastened it to my coat beneath the lapel.
“How foolish of you, Tess, to buy me something so beautiful,” I said.
“I didn’t buy it,” she said, laughing.
“Where did you get it?”
Then she told me how she had found it one day on her way from the Aquarium in the Battery. She had advertised it and watched the newspapers, but eventually gave up hope of finding its owner.
“That was last winter,” she said, “the very day I had the first horrible dream about the hearse.”
I remembered my dream of the night before but said nothing. Soon my charcoal was flying over a new canvas, and Tessie stood motionless on the model’s platform.
III

The following day was disastrous for me. While moving a framed canvas from one easel to another, I slipped on the polished floor and fell heavily on both wrists. They were so badly sprained that trying to hold a brush was useless. I could only wander about the studio, glaring at unfinished drawings and sketches. At last despair overcame me, and I sat down to smoke and twiddle my thumbs in a rage. Rain blew against the windows and rattled on the church roof. Its endless pattering drove me into a nervous fit. Tessie sat sewing by the window. Every now and then she raised her head and looked at me with such innocent sympathy that I began to feel ashamed of my irritation. I looked around for something to occupy me. I had read all the newspapers and every book in the library, but for something to do I went to the bookcases and pushed them open with my elbow. I knew every volume by its colour. I examined them all, moving slowly around the library and whistling to keep up my spirits. I was turning towards the dining room when I noticed a book bound in snakeskin, standing in a corner of the top shelf of the last bookcase. I did not remember it. From the floor I could not make out the pale lettering on its spine, so I went into the smoking room and called Tessie. She came in from the studio and climbed up to reach the book.
“What is it?” I asked.
“The King in Yellow.”

I was astonished. Who had put it there? How had it come into my rooms? Long ago I had decided never to open that book, and nothing on earth could have persuaded me to buy it. Afraid that curiosity might tempt me to open it, I had never even looked at it in bookshops. If I had ever been curious to read it, the terrible tragedy of young Castaigne, whom I knew, had stopped me from exploring its wicked pages. I had always refused to hear any description of it. Indeed, no one ever dared discuss the second part aloud, so I knew absolutely nothing of what those pages might reveal. I stared at the poisonous, mottled binding as I would have stared at a snake.
“Don’t touch it, Tessie,” I said. “Come down.”

Of course, my warning was enough to arouse her curiosity. Before I could stop her, she took the book and danced off into the studio, laughing. I called to her, but she slipped away with a teasing smile at my helpless hands. I followed, growing impatient.

“Tessie!” I cried as I entered the library. “Listen, I’m serious. Put that book away. I don’t want you to open it!” The library was empty. I searched both drawing rooms, then the bedrooms, laundry and kitchen. Finally I returned to the library and began a systematic search. She had hidden so well that half an hour passed before I found her crouching, white and silent, beside the latticed window in the storeroom upstairs. At a glance I saw that she had been punished for her foolishness. The King in Yellow lay at her feet, open at the second part. I looked at Tessie and saw that it was too late. She had opened The King in Yellow. I took her hand and led her to the studio. She seemed dazed. When I told her to lie on the sofa, she obeyed without a word. After a while she closed her eyes, and her breathing grew deep and regular, but I could not tell whether she was asleep. I sat silently beside her for a long time. She neither moved nor spoke. At last I stood up, went into the unused storeroom and picked up the book in my less injured hand. It seemed as heavy as lead, but I carried it back to the studio. Sitting on the rug beside the sofa, I opened it and read it through from beginning to end.
When, faint from the intensity of my emotions, I dropped the book and leaned wearily against the sofa, Tessie opened her eyes and looked at me.

We had been speaking in dull, monotonous voices for some time before I realised we were discussing The King in Yellow. Oh, the sin of writing such words—words clear as crystal, as pure and musical as bubbling springs, words sparkling and glowing like the Medicis’ poisoned diamonds! Oh, the wickedness, the hopeless damnation of a soul who could bewitch and paralyse human beings with such words! Words understood alike by the ignorant and the wise, more precious than jewels, more soothing than music, more terrible than death!

We kept talking, heedless of the gathering shadows. She begged me to throw away the black onyx clasp, strangely inlaid with what we now knew was the Yellow Sign. I will never know why I refused. Even now, here in my bedroom writing this confession, I would be glad to know what kept me from tearing the Yellow Sign from my chest and throwing it into the fire. I am sure I wanted to do it, yet Tessie pleaded in vain. Night fell, and the hours dragged on. Still we murmured to each other about the King and the Pallid Mask. Midnight sounded from the misty spires of the fog-wrapped city. We spoke of Hastur and Cassilda, while outside the fog rolled against the blank windowpanes as waves of cloud roll and break upon the shores of Hali.

The house was very silent now. Not a sound rose from the misty streets. Tessie lay among the cushions, her face a grey blot in the gloom, but her hands were clasped in mine. I knew that she knew and read my thoughts, as I read hers. For we had understood the mystery of the Hyades, and the Phantom of Truth had been laid to rest. Then, as we answered one another swiftly and silently, thought following thought, the shadows stirred in the gloom around us. Far away in the streets we heard a sound. Nearer and nearer it came, the dull crunch of wheels, nearer and nearer still. Now it stopped outside the door. I dragged myself to the window and saw a hearse with black plumes. The gate below opened and closed. Shaking, I crept to my door and bolted it, but I knew that no bolts or locks could keep out the creature coming for the Yellow Sign. Now I heard him moving very softly along the hall. Now he was at the door, and the bolts rotted at his touch. Now he had entered. With eyes bulging, I peered into the darkness, but when he came into the room I did not see him. Only when I felt him wrap me in his cold, soft grip did I cry out and struggle with deadly fury. But my hands were useless. He tore the onyx clasp from my coat and struck me squarely in the face. As I fell, I heard Tessie’s soft cry, and her spirit fled. Even as I fell, I longed to follow her. I knew that the King in Yellow had opened his tattered cloak, and now there was only God to cry to.

I could tell more, but I cannot see how it would help the world. As for me, I am beyond human help or hope. As I lie here writing, not even caring whether I die before I finish, I see the doctor gather his powders and little bottles. He makes a vague gesture towards the good priest beside me, and I understand it.

They will be very curious to learn of the tragedy—those in the outside world who write books and print millions of newspapers. But I will write no more. When the priest has completed his holy duty, he will seal my last words with the sacred seal of confession. Those in the outside world may send their creatures into ruined homes and households struck by death. Their newspapers will gorge themselves on blood and tears. But with me, their spies must stop at the confessional. They know Tessie is dead and I am dying. They know how an infernal scream roused the people in the house, who rushed into my room and found one living person and two dead. But they do not know what I will tell them now. They do not know that the doctor pointed to a horribly decomposed heap on the floor—the blue-grey corpse of the church watchman—and said, “I have no theory, no explanation. That man must have been dead for months!”
I think I am dying. I wish the priest would—
